intro: The three questions can now be placed beside the kind of variation each paper studies.
caption: Memory loss and eye drift concern changes over time; place-field statistics concern variation across a fixed spatial map. The eye pathway shows the proposed changing-command mechanism. Original guide schematic based on the three papers, with illustrative traces rather than recorded data.
alt: Three separate rows compare a wandering stored value over time, a proposed changing command passing through muscles to eye position, and one fixed spatial rate curve evaluated twice at the same place. They link to the 2012 memory, 2022 eye-drift and 2025 place-field papers respectively.
interpretation: The rows compare different questions; they do not establish a single circuit connecting all three papers.

intro: The exact trajectory in this example shows why the lasting displacement follows the flow rather than a perpendicular projection.
caption: Original guide construction of the tilted decay example, with dimensionless coordinates and $a/\lambda=1/2$. After an imposed jump from $(0,0)$ to $(0,2)$, the state relaxes toward $(1,0)$; successive time marks crowd toward that endpoint. This illustrates the left and right zero vector construction in Burak and Fiete (2012), Supporting Text, Section II, pp. 3–4, Eqs. S10–S16; it is not a paper network simulation.
alt: A line of fixed points lies at y equals zero. An imposed vertical jump from zero zero to zero two is followed by a straight tilted flow toward one zero. Equal time marks crowd toward the endpoint. Perpendicular projection would return to zero zero and miss the lasting shift of one. The tangent is one zero; the left vector measures delta x plus one half delta y.
interpretation: As y decays, x changes by one; the left vector extracts that lasting shift.

intro: A timeline separates the displacement accumulated before the cue from the error in estimating the cue state afterward.
caption: Original guide construction of storage and cue state readout, based on Burak and Fiete (2012), Supporting Text, p. 12, Eq. S57. The illustrated path is one possible construction, and the orange estimate concerns the state at the cue rather than the state at the end of observation. With the conditions shown, storage and readout variances add because their cross covariance is zero.
alt: The stored value starts at Theta at encoding time zero and wanders until the recall cue at T. Its cue value is x. Later spikes, collected through T plus L, give an estimate x hat of that cue state. Storage error is x minus Theta; readout error is x hat minus x. The estimate is drawn separately from the path endpoint. Under the listed independence, unbiasedness and translation assumptions, total variance is two D T plus readout variance.
interpretation: Later spikes can improve the estimate of $x=\theta(T)$; they do not reveal the particular storage displacements that separated $x$ from $\Theta$.

insert_after: Figure 3 isolates readout uncertainty, rescaling variance by $\sqrt{2D/J}$ and duration by $L^*$. In these axes the ideal curve is $\coth z$ and the naive curve is $z/3+1/z$. Both diverge like $1/z$ at short durations because too few spikes are available. The ideal solid curve approaches one. The naive dashed curve reaches $2/\sqrt3$ at $z=\sqrt3$, then rises because its equal weighting gives increasing importance to displaced states. The dotted vertical line marks that naive optimum. The storage delay contribution $2DT$ is not part of these rescaled curves. Figure S2 repeats the comparison for partial access, showing the rightward and upward shifts when $\alpha=0.1$.[^p1-fig3]
intro: The normalized curves make the eventual cost of equal weighting visible.
caption: Original guide construction from the analytic readout formulas in Burak and Fiete (2012), Fig. 3 and Supporting Text, Eqs. S75 and S79–S81, rather than digitized data. Ideal readout approaches a normalized variance of one; simple averaging reaches $2/\sqrt3$ at $z=\sqrt3$ and then worsens. These curves contain no storage variance $2DT$.
alt: Readout variance divided by square root of two D over J is plotted against z equals L times square root of two D J. Both curves diverge as z approaches zero. Ideal readout coth z falls toward one. Simple averaging z over three plus one over z reaches its minimum at square root of three, two over square root of three, and then rises. The storage variance is absent.
interpretation: More observation keeps helping the ideal reader, with diminishing benefit, while equal weighting eventually gives too much influence to a state that has moved.

anchor: The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell's activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect [**gain**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} during drift would change the inferred common variance. Gain is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other.
intro: The diagram separates the physical pathway from the paired recordings and the later calculation of predicted eye position.
caption: The recordings pair one motor neuron with eye movement. Private spike variability acts at individual cells, downstream physical variability acts on movement, and measurement noise enters the eye-position record. The attractor storage source is proposed; the dashed analysis path is a calculation from one cell through its calibrated filter. Original guide schematic based on Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figs. 1–2 and 4–5. Signal symbols are illustrative, not experimental traces.
alt: A proposed attractor storage circuit sends shared drive to a motor neuron population, then through muscles and eye mechanics to physical eye position. Private variability enters one neuron; downstream physical variability enters the muscles. Only the highlighted neuron is recorded, paired with eye position. Measurement noise enters that recorded position, not the physical eye. A separate dashed calculation transforms the single-cell spikes through a calibrated filter into predicted eye position.
interpretation: The upper path describes a possible physical source and its output. The recording design provides one cell and eye movement at a time; it does not measure covariance between simultaneously recorded motor neurons. The predicted position is a later analysis result, not a signal sent backward through the physical pathway.

intro: The curves compare the two inputs after the same filter with one exponential response, also called a one pole filter.
caption: Filtering stationary white input produces an MSD plateau; filtering Brownian stored position preserves long-lag growth. Each panel uses its own normalization, $M_{\mathrm{white}}/(A/\tau)$ and $M_{\mathrm{Brownian}}/(2D\tau)$, so the figure compares shapes without matching physical noise amplitudes. Original guide calculation for the one-pole teaching model, connected to Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Fig. 3 and main Eqs. 20–22; these are not measured data or the fitted full-model curves.
alt: Two alternative inputs pass through identical one-pole filters. On matched logarithmic lag axes x equals lag divided by tau, normalized white-input MSD is 1 minus exp(-x), rising with short-lag slope one and approaching a plateau of one. Independently normalized filtered Brownian MSD is x minus one plus exp(-x), starting with slope two and continuing to grow with long-lag slope one. The two vertical scales differ.
interpretation: The white-input short-lag slope of one belongs to this one-pole example.

Restricting to positive slopes counts only upward crossings. intro: A fixed smooth curve shows how to count a field already active at the left edge and why the crossing integral weights each slope.
caption: Two upcrossings start two new fields, and one field is already active at the left edge. The local tangent panels show that a steeper crossing occupies a narrower threshold band, while slope weighting makes each crossing contribute one. This is a guide construction, not a sampled cell or a new fit; it illustrates Mainali et al. (2025), Figure 1A–B and Supplemental Methods S3, Equations S11–S15.
alt: A constructed smooth curve crosses q upward twice and has three active intervals because the first begins before the left edge of the track. One full field and one gap are marked. Two local tangent plots use the same vertical band q plus or minus epsilon; the steeper slope has a narrower horizontal width 2 epsilon divided by v, and slope times width divided by 2 epsilon equals one in both cases.
interpretation: The count includes every connected active interval intersecting the track. Discarding clipped boundary fields would change this convention.

anchor: The density $p_{z,z'}(q,v)$ describes how often height is near $q$ and slope near $v$. Multiplication by $v$ compensates for the shorter spatial window of a steep crossing. intro: The same local radius gives a length, an area, or a volume depending on the dimension of the region.
caption: In the high-threshold approximation, excess peak height fixes a radius, and converting that radius into length, area, or volume gives powers 2, 1, and 2/3 in $U=\beta s^{2/d}$. The round regions are a guide reconstruction of the limiting geometry, not observed field shapes; see Mainali et al. (2025), Equation 1 and Supplemental Methods S4, with the parabola constants checked in this chapter.
alt: A local parabola stands epsilon above threshold q, and its full width is twice r star. U equals q times epsilon and r star is approximately square root of two times sigma divided by q times square root of U. The same radius gives an interval of length 2 r star, a disk of area pi r star squared, or a ball of volume four pi r star cubed over three. Therefore U depends on size to powers 2, 1, and 2/3.
interpretation: The changing power comes from geometry. The round shape and exponential excess belong to the high-threshold limit, so they do not make every measured place field spherical.
author_check: Viewed final original-size and 700-pixel PNGs. Radius, full width, epsilon and q are distinct. Moved the three size formulas below the shapes to remove crowding.
expert_objection: Using an exactly round blob could hide finite-threshold shape fluctuations. Resolution: the image says local high-peak approximation, and the caption and interpretation explicitly limit the construction.

insert_after: The [**Euler characteristic**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, written $\chi$, combines these counts. In 1D it equals the number of connected active intervals. In 2D it is the number of connected components minus the number of independent holes. Three disjoint disks have $\chi=3$; one connected ring has $\chi=1-1=0$. In 3D it is components minus independent tunnels plus enclosed cavities. A solid ball has $\chi=1$, a solid ring has $\chi=0$, and a hollow spherical shell has $\chi=2$. These counts are the first three [**Betti numbers**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: numbers of independent components, loops, and cavities, respectively.[^p3-ec-source]
intro: Thresholding one fixed smooth map separates the number of connected fields from the number of holes.
caption: As the threshold rises on one constructed smooth map, components and holes change separately, giving Euler characteristics -1, 0, 4, and 3. The above-threshold regions shrink as the threshold rises, even though this signed count does not change in one direction. This guide example is not an observed place-field map or a Gaussian-process sample; it illustrates Mainali et al. (2025), Figure 3F–H and STAR Methods Equations 8–10.
alt: Four thresholds of the same smooth two-dimensional map show one component with two holes and chi minus one; one component with one hole and chi zero; four components with no holes and chi four; and three components with no holes and chi three. Each active set is contained in the preceding one as q increases from 0.3 to 0.5, 0.8 and 1.0.
interpretation: A negative chi means that holes outnumber components in this 2D example. It does not mean a negative number of fields. When holes are absent, chi equals the component count.
author_check: Viewed final original-size and 700-pixel PNGs. Both holes at q=0.3, the single joined hole at q=0.5, the fourth small component at q=0.8 and its disappearance at q=1 are visible. Counts match connected-mask calculations at two resolutions.
expert_objection: A sequence of unrelated shapes could wrongly suggest thresholding one map, and raster connectivity can change near a saddle. Resolution: every mask uses the same explicit analytic smooth function, nesting is checked elementwise, and counts agree on 701 and 1001 grids. All activity stays away from the domain boundary.
